documents.evidence: Both versions let makers claim boards before similar bowls arrive, keep rear access for deep shelves, and light the back to reveal low dishes. Both show beginners hand-sized gaps before loading, remove damaged boards immediately to protect platters, and give staff a named contact during a member’s absence.

The dated chair counts still let organizers judge capacity, and both collection and return times are requested at booking because use may extend into Sunday. The reachable keyholder, inspection and cleaning interval, repair tag plus separate storage, and alternate returner if the organizer leaves early all retain their purposes.

The rewrite retains separate lines when both overlapping voices are intelligible, a size-adjustable sample at every station before a long interview, and visible captions from the opening words. Topic links still skip to passages, optional listing notes preserve the listener’s place, and the title still identifies a looping story to someone joining midway.

The original asks the host to announce the type of dance. “Name each dance” could mean naming its type or announcing a particular dance by title, which may leave a beginner unsure what kind it is. The advance timing, invitation and decline, low turn, visual cues, payment details, and quieter social break otherwise retain their purposes.

The original asks each baker for a next-day serving suggestion and leaves open when to collect it. “As people choose, ask bakers” moves collection to the selection period, which matters if the organizer collects suggestions before visitors arrive. The portion sizes, labeling, family activity, consent for spare bread, and suggestions for the next gathering survive.

Both use an unfinished opening sketch to encourage imperfect public marks and scrap paper for private practice. The viewfinder still frames a manageable patch, the binding frees a hand to steady a child, location notes help others find plants, and turning the book toward the plant keeps other guests out of photographs.

Garment and wearer-side labels still support the next day’s sewing, the dedicated rail keeps stage-ready pieces apart at cleanup, and the visible clock keeps the fitter’s attention on the performer. Owner limits still protect borrowed hems. Repeat fittings are circled and scheduled with the wearer while their schedule and garment are present, and excess work still triggers written priorities tied to rehearsal.

The demonstration board still prevents crowds at active games, the entrance-facing sign identifies willing opponents, and the busy-period list lets visitors read while waiting. Long post-game analysis still happens away from quiet boards, a private word with the host can resolve rules disputes, and noting a paused position frees the board.
